edge.title: The accidental ₹8,000
edge.setup: ₹8,000 lands in your account. A distressed message follows: wrong number, elderly mother's medicine money, please return. The transaction is real — you can see it. They ask you to send it back to a different UPI ID than the one it came from, or via a link they share.
edge.tell: They want the refund to go somewhere other than exactly where it came from.
move: Never return it yourself. Call your bank, report an unknown credit, let the bank reverse it.
If the money came from a stolen account or a loan app, your voluntary transfer makes you the visible link in the chain.
Screenshot everything before you touch anything.
edge.why: The money is usually stolen or borrowed in someone else's name. You are being recruited as a mule — an account that launders it one hop further. The bank reversal costs you nothing; the manual refund hands them a clean path and leaves your name on it.
edge.variants: Same shape: 'extra salary credited by mistake', refund-for-cancelled-order overpayments, 'I sent you the full amount, send back the difference'.

lens.name: Compounding
lens.one_line: Small consistent changes beat big sporadic ones, because the result is multiplicative, not additive.
lens.detail: Intuition is linear; compounding isn't, which is why almost everyone underestimates it. ₹5,000 a month at 12% is about ₹11 lakh in 10 years and roughly ₹50 lakh in 20 — most of that gain arriving in the final stretch. The same shape governs skills, reputation and debt. Credit-card interest at 3.5% a month is this force running against you at roughly 50% a year.
elsewhere: Minimum card payments keeping a balance alive for years.
Reputation: slow to build, then suddenly everything arrives at once.
lens.test: Is this a one-time event, or something that multiplies? Multiplying things deserve disproportionate attention.
lens.today: A Bengaluru man paid ₹12,500 a month for 40 months into a ₹5 lakh chit scheme and received only ₹20,000; the consumer commission has ordered ₹4.07 lakh with interest (The Times of India). Small, regular payments feel harmless, yet 40 of them is ₹5 lakh, and the same multiplying works for whoever holds the money. Before joining any monthly scheme, add up the full total you will pay.

moved.what: Karnataka is raising milk prices by ₹8 per litre from 1 November; farmers get ₹7 of it (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: Expect your monthly milk bill to rise from 1 November. If you buy by monthly subscription, recheck the new rate before the next renewal.

moved.what: The Pink Line has safety clearance and PM Modi may inaugurate it on 15 November (Swarajya, Udayavani); The Hindu reports it opens only if the PM visits.
moved.so_what: Treat 15 November as likely, not confirmed. Do not change a commute or house plan until BMRCL announces public opening.

moved.what: IKEA's second Bengaluru store, an 80,000-sq-ft city store, opens on 5 November, near Konanakunte metro (Moneycontrol, Urban Acres).
moved.so_what: If you are furnishing a home, expect a crowd in the opening week; go on a weekday, or after the first fortnight.

moved.what: 83,806 voter enrolment requests were rejected, and only 9 of 361 appeals against deletions have been heard (The Times of India).
moved.so_what: If you applied or were deleted, check your status on the Election Commission portal and keep the acknowledgement. Appeals are slow, so file early.

moved.what: The GBA plans a month-long cleanliness drive from 1 November, and a 'One Ward, One Drive' campaign targets neighbourhood issues (Deccan Herald, The New Indian Express).
moved.so_what: If a garbage blackspot or broken stretch near you has been ignored, report it now while the drive is running.

moved.what: 61-metre girders have been installed over NH-44 near Chandapura for the Bengaluru–Hosur rail project (The New Indian Express, Asianet Newsable).
moved.so_what: Expect work-zone slowdowns on Hosur Road and add buffer time for airport or office trips that use it.

carry_over.prompt: Someone near you in a crowded metro coach holds a phone still, lens toward you, thumb nowhere near the screen: what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: A phone held still with the lens toward you and no one touching the screen.
